passage: On the last night of his leave, Pradeep sat on the bund of his father's sugarcane field outside Mandya, the offer email from the Bengaluru firm still open on his phone. Two more years there, and a promotion. Or come home, as Appa half-hoped, and try the drip-irrigation idea he had sketched on a napkin. Dhruv, who had stayed and now ran a small dairy with twelve cows, walked up with two glasses of buttermilk. "Still thinking?" "Whichever I pick, I feel I've failed at the other." Dhruv laughed. "I stayed. Nobody calls it failing now. You went. Nobody calls that failing either." Pradeep looked at the lights of the town. "What would I give here? What would I get?" He took out a pen and began two lists on the back of the napkin.

qa.q: How many cows does Dhruv's dairy have?
qa.a: Dhruv's dairy has twelve cows.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as he sat on the bund?
qa.a: Pradeep felt torn and uneasy, afraid that choosing either path would feel like failing at the other.

qa.q: What small step is Pradeep taking toward a wise choice?
qa.a: Writing two lists of what he would give and get in each place turns a vague fear of failing into a choice based on his values and chances.

qa.q: How does Dhruv see the choice between staying and leaving?
qa.a: Dhruv sees neither as failure; having stayed himself, he knows both paths can earn respect.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional weighing a city job against returning to family land, seeing that neither is failure and the choice rests on values and what he can give and get.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. Yamini, room teacher.
Nilesh arrived clinging to his mother's dupatta and would not let go for twenty minutes. She said they are packing for the move to Pune and the flat is full of boxes. He cried when I took his blue bottle to wash, so I gave it straight back. He settled once he had the bottle and his usual song at nap time. What I did next: asked his mother to pack his bedsheet and bottle last, and unpack them first.

qa.q: What made Nilesh cry at daycare?
qa.a: He cried when his blue bottle was taken to wash.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh clinging to his mother's dupatta?
qa.a: He was probably anxious and unsettled by the boxes and the move, and wanted to stay close to someone familiar.

qa.q: Why was packing the bedsheet and bottle last a good idea?
qa.a: Those familiar things will be the first ones out in the new flat, giving Nilesh a sense of security in a strange place.

qa.q: What might the move feel like for Nilesh's mother?
qa.a: She is probably busy and a little stressed with the packing, and may feel relieved to have a simple plan to help him settle.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler clinging more during a family move and how familiar objects and routines give him security.

passage:
Monday. Farida's first day in Bengaluru. The maths class was two chapters ahead of her old school in Lucknow, and when the teacher said something in Kannada, everyone laughed except her. She ate her tiffin alone by the water tank.
Thursday. Nilesh, who sat behind her, pushed his notebook across. "We did fractions last month. Copy the examples, I'll explain at break." At home Ammi kept their Lucknow routine: tea at five, homework at the dining table, a story before bed. Farida fell asleep without crying for the first time.
The next Monday. Farida walked in and said "Namaskara" to the watchman, the one Kannada word Nilesh had taught her. He grinned from the gate. At break they shared her sheermal and his chakli.

qa.q: What word did Farida say to the watchman?
qa.a: She said "Namaskara" to the watchman.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on her first day, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt lonely and out of place, eating her tiffin alone by the water tank after missing the Kannada joke.

qa.q: Which two things helped Farida settle, and why?
qa.a: Nilesh's help with fractions gave her a friend at school, and Ammi's steady Lucknow routine made home feel safe.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have noticed that made him offer his notebook?
qa.a: Nilesh likely noticed she was behind in maths and alone, and was kind enough to help without making a fuss.

grounding: It illustrates a child struggling with language, syllabus and friends after a family move, helped most by a kind classmate and a steady home routine.

passage: You asked how it is, living with Aaji and Ajoba. I'm Santosh, and it's been three years since Papa went to work in Muscat. I know why he went. The loan on the house, my sister's college. I know. But on my birthday last year he called four hours late, and I didn't pick up. I told my friend Harish I didn't care. That wasn't true. Ajoba found me on the terrace that night and didn't lecture. He said, "Tell your father what you told the terrace." So on Sunday I did. Papa went quiet, then said he misses my voice more than anything over there. Now we have a fixed call, Sunday, nine o'clock, and he tells me the boring parts of his week too. It still hurts sometimes. It just doesn't feel like anger any more.

qa.q: When is the fixed call with Papa?
qa.a: The fixed call is on Sunday, at nine o'clock.

qa.q: Why didn't Santosh pick up the late birthday call?
qa.a: Santosh was hurt and angry that Papa called four hours late, even while understanding why Papa works away.

qa.q: What made the difference between loneliness and resentment here?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Papa, nudged by Ajoba, and setting a regular Sunday call turned silent hurt into steady contact.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Santosh finally spoke honestly?
qa.a: Papa likely felt sad and moved, going quiet and then saying he misses Santosh's voice more than anything over there.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager living with grandparents while a parent works abroad, whose loneliness is kept from turning into resentment by honest talk and regular calls.

passage: People ask me about Kota and expect a sad story. I'm Arnab, and the truth is both things at once. The first week, I was thrilled. No one telling me when to sleep, egg rolls at midnight, my own shelf. Then the nights came. Around eleven the corridor goes quiet, and I could smell Ma's fish curry from memory, and I'd scroll old photos till two. My roommate Pradeep noticed my eyes in the morning and said nothing, just started waking me at six for a walk to the tea stall. We made rules: bed by twelve, walk at six, call home every Wednesday and Sunday. Ma now asks about Pradeep before she asks about me. The homesickness hasn't gone. But it's a visitor now, not the landlord.

qa.q: What time did Pradeep start waking Arnab?
qa.a: Pradeep started waking Arnab at six.

qa.q: How did Arnab's feelings in the first week differ from the nights?
qa.a: Arnab felt thrilled by the freedom in the first week but homesick and lonely at night, missing Ma's fish curry.

qa.q: Which routines made Arnab's move steadier?
qa.a: Going to bed by twelve, walking at six with Pradeep, and calling home every Wednesday and Sunday.

qa.q: How might Ma feel about Arnab's new routine?
qa.a: Ma seems reassured and fond, asking about Pradeep first, glad that Arnab is no longer alone.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult in a hostel far from home who is thrilled by freedom and homesick at night, steadied by routines, a friend and regular calls.

passage: The water in Block C went off on the Monday of Gautam's first exam week, and he had one clean shirt left. He had shrunk the other two in the hostel machine on the hot cycle. His roommates, strangers from Assam and Kerala, were still asleep. He had also spent most of his monthly allowance in the first fortnight on canteen parathas. At seven he found his lab partner Damini hanging washing on the line outside the girls' block. "How do you make the money last?" he asked, embarrassed. Damini laughed kindly. "The mess is cheaper than the canteen. And cold wash, always. Everyone ruins shirts in first year." That night Gautam asked his roommates to share a bucket of water from the tanker. They ended up cooking instant noodles on a borrowed kettle and finally learnt each other's names properly.

qa.q: How did Gautam shrink his shirts?
qa.a: He shrank them in the hostel machine on the hot cycle.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel asking Damini for help?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about his mistakes, yet trusted Damini enough to ask, and was likely relieved by her kind laugh.

qa.q: What does Gautam's week show about hostel mistakes?
qa.a: Mistakes like shrunken shirts and a thin wallet turn into lessons once he asks for help, from Damini and from his roommates.

qa.q: How might Gautam's roommates see him after the water cut?
qa.a: They probably find him friendlier and easier to live with, since his asking to share water led to cooking together and learning names.

grounding: It illustrates a student handling laundry, food and money alone for the first time in a shared room, learning from mistakes and finding that asking for help is a strength.

passage: On salary day, Sabina sat in the office pantry with her phone, sending the usual transfer home to Siliguri. Her brother's school fees, Abba's medicines, the roof. She felt the small warm pride she always felt, and then, a minute later, a tightness in her chest. Her own rent was due on Friday. Hansa, from accounts, set down two cups of tea. "You look like someone who has just paid everyone except herself." Sabina laughed, then didn't. "If I send less, Ammi will think I've changed. If I don't, I can't breathe here." "Have you ever told her the numbers? Your side, I mean." "No. It feels rude." "It might feel like trust to her." That evening Sabina called home and, for the first time, said out loud what the city cost her.

qa.q: Where did Sabina send the transfer?
qa.a: She sent it home to Siliguri.

qa.q: What did Sabina feel after sending the money?
qa.a: Sabina felt proud and warm at first, then a tight worry in her chest because her own rent was due.

qa.q: What did Hansa suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Hansa suggested sharing Sabina's side of the numbers with Ammi, since open talk about what can be kept up prevents quiet resentment.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when Sabina explains what the city costs?
qa.a: Ammi may be surprised at first, but could also feel trusted and relieved to understand, rather than thinking Sabina has changed.

grounding: It illustrates a young worker who sends part of a salary home with both pride and heavy duty, and begins to talk openly with family about what is sustainable.

passage: I'm Rekha, and this is something I only noticed this year. Every Sunday I call home from Hyderabad, and Appa's voice jumps ten feet when he hears it's me. "Rekha-ma! Eaten?" Then, very fast, he says everything is fine, the knees are fine, the neighbours are fine, go, go, you must be busy. For two years I believed him. Then in March my cousin sent a photo: Appa sitting alone on the verandah, two tumblers of coffee beside him, one untouched. That was Amma's habit, before she passed. I sat on the floor of my flat for a long time. Now I call on Wednesdays too, just to hear him complain about the milkman. And I've booked leave for Pongal. He said, "Why waste leave?" His voice was shaking.

qa.q: What did the cousin's photo show?
qa.a: It showed Appa sitting alone on the verandah with two tumblers of coffee beside him, one untouched.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel after seeing the photo?
qa.a: Rekha feels shaken and sad, sitting on the floor for a long time, seeing that Appa's cheerful "fine" was hiding loneliness.

qa.q: What did Rekha do once the quiet longing was clear?
qa.a: Rekha added a Wednesday call just to chat and booked leave for Pongal, giving regular contact and a visit.

qa.q: Why might Appa keep saying everything is fine?
qa.a: Appa probably does not want to burden Rekha and hides his loneliness out of love, though his shaking voice about the leave shows how much the visit means.

grounding: It illustrates a parent who lights up at a call but hides loneliness, and a young adult who reads it and calls more often and plans a visit.

passage:
Chetan's diary. Toronto, Saturday, week 6.
Minus twelve today. I bought the wrong bus pass again, and the driver explained the zones very slowly, like I was a child, but kindly. Groceries cost what a week of dinners did at home. Nobody here asks where I'm from the way uncles ask; nobody asks anything. I like that. I also hate it.
At 4 pm I video-called Shankar and the whole gang at our old tea stall in Pune. They held the phone up to the rain. I laughed and then felt empty for an hour.
Then Mateo from the lab knocked. He'd made too much chili and said I looked like I needed beans. We ate on the floor and compared our mothers' cooking. He's from Monterrey, homesick too.
Tomorrow: the Sunday cricket group at the community centre. And call Aai.

qa.q: Where is Mateo from?
qa.a: Mateo is from Monterrey.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel after the video call with Shankar and the gang?
qa.a: Chetan laughed during it but then felt empty and homesick for an hour.

qa.q: What is Chetan doing to build a steadier life abroad?
qa.a: Chetan is accepting local friendship, like dinner with Mateo and the Sunday cricket group, while keeping ties home through calls to the gang and Aai.

qa.q: What might it be like for Mateo to knock on Chetan's door?
qa.a: Mateo, homesick too, probably wanted company as much as Chetan did, and sharing food eased loneliness for both.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult abroad facing new rules, costs and loneliness, feeling both free and unrooted, and building local friendships while keeping ties home.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage: Jasleen, you're scared the neighbours heard you shouting at your brother? Let me tell you something. When I was nine, I broke the Sharmas' flowerpot with my cricket ball. My mother didn't ask if I had said sorry. She grabbed my arm and whispered, "What will people say? The whole gali will talk." So I learnt to hide things. The next time I broke something, a cycle bell, I buried it behind the water tank. I wasn't sorry; I was scared of being seen. Years later my teacher, Master Iqbal, caught me copying. He didn't mention anyone else's opinion. He just asked, "Is it right?" That question stayed with me longer than all the gossip. So ask yourself that one, Jasleen. Your Chaitanya Dadu is still learning it.

qa.q: What did young Chaitanya bury behind the water tank?
qa.a: He buried a cycle bell he had broken.

qa.q: What did young Chaitanya feel when he buried the cycle bell?
qa.a: He felt scared of being seen rather than sorry, which shows shame had taught him fear, not conscience.

qa.q: At the turning point, why did Master Iqbal's question work better than "What will people say?"
qa.a: "Is it right?" made Chaitanya judge his own action instead of worrying about gossip, which built a conscience that lasted.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya's mother have reacted with "What will people say?"
qa.a: She was probably embarrassed and worried about the family's name in the gali, so her first fear was the neighbours' talk, not the lesson.

grounding: It illustrates a child warned that a mistake will make the neighbours talk, who learns to fear being seen before understanding right and wrong.
